lesson_title: Moving a River Over a Mountain: How Gauteng Gets Its Water
hook_text: Johannesburg's water starts as snow in another country — and flows there without a single pump.
clip_script: Gauteng has a problem no planner would choose: South Africa's biggest cluster of people, mines and factories sits high on a plateau with no great river. So engineers did something audacious — they went and fetched a river from another country. Look east to Lesotho, the roof of southern Africa. Two facts are true up there: it rains and snows more than almost anywhere in the region, and the land stands far HIGHER than Johannesburg. Those two facts are the entire scheme. Build dams high in the Maluti mountains — Katse, curved like a shield across its valley, and Mohale. Bore tunnels straight through the mountains. Then let physics do the freight: the water runs downhill, underground, kilometre after kilometre, across the border and into the rivers that feed the Vaal — no pumps, no power bill. Gauteng drinks; Lesotho earns royalties that rank among its biggest incomes, plus electricity from the falling water itself. Compare the hard way: the Thukela river flows at the BOTTOM of the escarpment, so its water must be PUMPED up the mountain wall into Sterkfontein Dam — so expensive it is saved as the national drought reserve. One law explains both: gravity is free, and fighting gravity costs a fortune.
visual_style: Sweeping aerial of the Maluti mountains and the curved Katse wall; an animated cross-section of water dropping through tunnels from high Lesotho down to the Vaal; a contrasting red arrow forced up the escarpment to Sterkfontein.
pacing: Problem stated fast, the two facts landed hard, the tunnel journey savoured, the pumped contrast as a sharp closer.
